Take-Home Exercise 1

Author

Amelia Rosalind

Published

May 22, 2026

Modified

May 23, 2026

Overview

The data used is a real-world vehicle insurance data from Spanish insurance company, comprising 254,140 policy records spanning from 2022 to 2024. The objective is to gain deeper insights into data distributions using univariate analysis and understand key factors influencing profitability and volatility using bivariate analysis. This technical report will cover the technical working of this project, such as data preprocessing and all analyses done.

Getting Started

Installing of required packages

pacman::p_load(ggstatsplot, tidyverse, knitr,
               patchwork, ggthemes, ggdist)

Importing data

insurance <- read_delim("Motor_insurance.csv",
                        delim = ";",
                        col_types = cols(.default = "c"))

Problems

  1. All features are now characters so need to change the data type of the numerical values into numeric.

  2. Some features have nulls: vehicle_value has 513 NAs, fuel_type has 1287 NAs, fire_incurred has 94 NAs, occupants_incurred has 25 NAs.

  3. Categoricals (policy_type, policy_status, business_type, payment_frequency, bonus_score, fuel_type, municipality_type, circulation_area, vehicle_brand) are stored as characters instead of factors . With data type factors, R will understand that it is categoricals and not some string.

Data Wrangling

Cleaning the data

insurance <- insurance %>%
  # Fix numerical columns' data type
  mutate(across(c(insured_id, year, driver_age, vehicle_age,
                  age_driving_licence, vehicle_value, 
                  seats, power_to_weight_ratio,
                  total_premium, total_claims,
                  liability_claims, 
                  liability_property_claims,
                  liability_injury_claims, property_claims,
                  theft_claims, fire_claims, glass_claims,
                  legal_protection_claims, occupants_claims,
                  total_incurred, liability_incurred,
                  liability_property_incurred,
                  liability_injury_incurred,
                  property_incurred, theft_incurred,
                  fire_incurred, glass_incurred,
                  legal_protection_incurred,
                  occupants_incurred, liability_premium,
                  property_damage_premium, theft_premium,
                  fire_premium, glass_premium,
                  legal_protection_premium,
                  occupants_premium, total_exposure,
                  liability_exposure),
                ~ as.numeric(.))) %>%
  # Convert categoricals to factors
  mutate(across(c(policy_type, policy_status, business_type,
                  payment_frequency,bonus_score, fuel_type,
                  municipality_type, circulation_area,
                  vehicle_brand),
                as.factor)) %>%
  drop_na()

Feature Engineering

driving_experience

driving_experience is needed to get how long the driver has been driving for, which is more meaningful as compared to the age when the driver receives the driving licence.

First check if age_driving_licence means the year driving licence is issued or the age the driver got the driving licence.

insurance %>%
  filter(age_driving_licence == 80) %>%
  select(driver_age, age_driving_licence, year)
# A tibble: 1 × 3
  driver_age age_driving_licence  year
       <dbl>               <dbl> <dbl>
1         82                  80  2024

Combining with the first row value shown in the head summary, it can be concluded that age_driving_licence is the age of the driver when driving licence is issued. Hence to get driving_experience the formula should be driver_age - age_driving_licence.

insurance <- insurance %>%
  mutate(driving_experience = 
           driver_age - age_driving_licence)

loss_ratio

This feature will show the ratio of total_incurred to total_premium. This is important as it is the standard insurance profitability metric.

insurance <- insurance %>%
  mutate(loss_ratio = total_incurred / total_premium)

There is a possibility that the total_premium is 0 which will produce Inf or NaN instead of a value, so check next.

sum(is.infinite(insurance$loss_ratio))
[1] 1
sum(is.nan(insurance$loss_ratio))
[1] 48

Since there is only a total of 49 values Inf or NaN, dropping rows with them is negligible.

insurance <- insurance %>%
  mutate(loss_ratio = ifelse(is.infinite(loss_ratio) | is.nan(loss_ratio), 
                             NA, loss_ratio)) %>%
  drop_na(loss_ratio)

sum(is.infinite(insurance$loss_ratio))
[1] 0
sum(is.nan(insurance$loss_ratio))
[1] 0
nrow(insurance)
[1] 352289

The final dataset now have 352,289 rows remaining, and 48 columns in total with the new column made. The data types are also all correct.

Variable selection

Profitability is about how much profit the insurance company can make from a policy, which is addressed with loss_ratio. Volatility concerns the spread and unpredictability of losses, which can be addressed by total_incurred. As such the target variables are loss_ratio and total_incurred.

Other variables that can help explain profitability and volatility are listed on the table below

Variable Description Purpose
total_premium Revenue collected per policy Provides context on income side of portfolio
total_claims Number of claims made Indicates claim frequency which directly drives costs
driver_age Age of driver Older or younger drivers may present different risk profiles
vehicle_age Age of the insured vehicle Older vehicles may be more probe to certain types of claims
driving_experience Years of driving experience More experienced drivers may have lower claim rates
policy_type Types coverage held Different coverage types carry different risk exposures and premium levels
bonus_score Claims history indicator Drivers with poor claims history are likely higher risk
circulation_area Urban vs rural driving environment Urban areas typically have higher accident rates

Univariate Analysis

Distribution of target variables

  • Volatibility
  • Profitability

    Min.  1st Qu.   Median     Mean  3rd Qu.     Max. 
     0.0      0.0      0.0    208.4      0.0 571128.3 
box_cost <- ggplot(insurance, aes(y = total_incurred, x = "")) +
  geom_boxplot(outlier.colour="lightgreen") +
  geom_point(aes(x = "", 
                 y = mean(insurance$total_incurred)),
             colour = "red", 
             size = 2, 
             shape = 18) +
  coord_flip() +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(-1e+05, 6e+05)) +
  labs(title = "Distribution of Total Incurred (Cost)") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    axis.text = element_blank(), 
    axis.ticks = element_blank(),
    axis.title = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.major = element_blank(),
    plot.background = element_rect(fill="white",
                                   colour="white")
  )

hist_cost <- ggplot(insurance, aes(x = total_incurred)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 50,
                 colour = "grey25",
                 fill = "grey90") +
  geom_vline(aes(xintercept = mean(total_incurred)), 
             color = "red", linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_vline(aes(xintercept = median(total_incurred)), 
             color = "blue", linetype = "dashed") +
  scale_x_continuous(limits = c(-1e+05, 6e+05)) +
  labs(x = "total_incurred") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    axis.text.y = element_blank(),
    axis.title.y = element_blank(),
    plot.background = element_rect(fill="white",
                                   colour="white")
  )

hbox <- (box_cost / hist_cost) +
  plot_layout(heights = c(1.5, 3.5))

hbox & theme(plot.background = element_rect(fill="white",colour="white"))
Note

There are a lot of zeros as compared to the others, as majority have no claims made. This is known as zero-inflation.
